# Methods

In the first instance, I'll use R along with the OpenAir tools, see if that's possible. As a citizen science group, this Methods document is written for a citizen scientist audience, to share learning about working with climate data.

## Temperature

Some key figures about predicted change came from the Met Office website LCAT tool, where the user can specify Edinburgh (and/or Scotland) and the tool generates a detailed report with stats for that area.

Drew two lines onto the temperature bar chart to read the axis.

[![Temperature bar chart with manually added grid lines](images/annotated%20EUROPE-United_Kingdom-Edinburgh-1850-2024-BK-barslabel.png){fig-alt="Two lines on the bar chart show temperature increase of 1.3 degrees by 2022 and 1.0 by 2024."}](https://www.reading.ac.uk/planet/climate-resources/climate-stripes)

We did attempt to extract temperature data from the CEDA archive. This was quite challenging, despite starting with a good level of R knowledge. The Hadley UK grid data is in netcdf format, a very well-established standard in the academic community. However, there was a surprising lack of good resources for help on how to pick out temperatures for a given geographical location, and date, using R. There's definitely an opportunity for someone (maybe Hadley Centre / CEDA themselves) to signpost or create a simple exemplar or even a tutorial.

# Data Sources
